newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH PARLIAMENT KILLS OPPOSITION PENSION BILL.
newsitem.headline: CZECH PARLIAMENT KILLS OPPOSITION PENSION BILL.

text.p: The lower house of the Czech parliament voted on Wednesday rejected a plan by the opposition Social Democratic party to lower the pension age, the house's press office told Reuters.

The plan, on which the centre-right ruling Civic Democratic Party (ODS) once threatened to resign if appproved, failed in a preliminary vote in the house 100 to 98, with two absentions, Mariana Cerna of the press department said.

The ruling coalition has already implemented a measure to gradually raise the retirment age from communist-era levels for men to 62 by 2007 from age 60 currently, and to 58 to 61 for women from 54 to 57, depending on the number of children they had.
The opposition proposal would have kept the communist-era pension ages in place.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus said last December his ruling ODS would walk out of the three-party governing coalition if his partners backed opposition plans to lower the pension age and boost farm subsidies.

The Social Democratic pension proposal passed through the parliament's first of three readings at the end of the last year due to support of some deputies for junior coalition partner, the centrist Christian Democrats (KDU-CSL).

Klaus in December said the KDU-CSL had violated a coalition agreement by supporting the measure in the first reading, and warned of a potential collapse of Czech post-Communist reforms if the plans were adopted.
Klaus said keeping the pension age lower would bring budget imbalances and unbearable burden for taxpayers.
The government pushed through its 1997 balanced budget plan, but difficulities with tax collection have brought it to a 7.9 billion crowns deficit at the beginning of this week.
Some economists have called for a switch to a fund-based pension system, warning that raising retirement age would not help much to frinance the pay-as-you-go system in the long run.
